analysis.one_liner: Limits the interest deductions inverted companies use to shift US profits offshore.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: introduced in March 2016, referred to Finance the same day, and it expired without a vote when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a US company moves its headquarters abroad on paper to lower its tax bill (an 'inversion'), it often loads its US subsidiary with debt and deducts the interest, stripping taxable profits out of the country. This bill would cap those interest deductions at 25% of adjusted taxable income for such companies, deny them carryforwards of disallowed interest, count any company less than half-owned by its US shareholders as an inverter, and require ten years of annual IRS agreements covering their deals with foreign affiliates — with deduction bans if they fail to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary US taxpayers, who keep revenue that would otherwise be lost to profit-shifting, and domestic companies that compete against inverted firms without the same tax break.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the interest deduction of inverted corporations at 25% of adjusted taxable income, with no carryforward of disallowed interest in the first covered year, reducing a main channel for shifting US profits offshore.
Broadens the definition of an inverter to companies where former US owners hold more than 50% (rather than 60%), and applies it to past as well as future inversions.

Requires applicable entities to file an annual IRS approval agreement for ten years after inversion; if they fail, they lose deductions for transactions with foreign related parties, disregarded intangible transfers, and cost-sharing arrangements.

analysis.who_pays: Inverted multinational corporations — many in pharmaceuticals, technology, and other industries — which would face sharply higher US tax bills and a new annual compliance regime.

drawbacks.text: The 25% interest cap could raise financing costs for the US operations of inverted firms and, by extension, discourage some borrowing and investment in those US operations.
The annual approval-agreement requirement creates a heavy compliance burden and gives the Treasury Secretary significant discretion over which related-party deals are approved.
The bill is narrow: it targets only companies that have actually inverted, leaving similar interest-based profit shifting by other multinationals untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted, modest crack-down on one specific tax-avoidance route — interest stripping by inverted companies — rather than a broad corporate tax overhaul. The revenue and fairness gains are real but limited in scope, and the main costs are higher compliance burdens and financing costs for the affected firms. On balance it favors ordinary taxpayers, though its narrowness means most corporate profit-shifting channels would continue.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Schumer introduced the bill on March 10, 2016, joined by Democratic senators Durbin, Brown, Cardin, Nelson, Stabenow, Menendez, and Warren.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, which is the last action recorded for the bill.
No markup, hearing, or floor vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died at the end of the 114th Congress in January 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Inverted multinational corporations, which kept the existing rules allowing interest deductions that shift US profits offshore. No revenue was raised because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Inverted multinationals kept the old rules

for.name: Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or any consideration of the bill after it was referred to Finance.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors were Democrats (8 of 44 Senate Democrats), no Republican cosponsored it, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Inverted multinational corporations (pharmaceutical, technology and other firms that redomiciled abroad)
industries.note: These companies rely on interest deductions paid to foreign affiliates to move US profits into low-tax jurisdictions; the bill caps that deduction and adds an annual IRS approval regime. Their interest runs against ordinary taxpayers, who bear the revenue loss when profits escape US tax.

industries.industry: Domestic US companies competing against inverted firms
industries.note: By tightening the rules for inverters, the bill narrows a tax advantage their non-inverted competitors do not enjoy.
